newsitem.title: UK: Europe unites on time, France poised to step back.
newsitem.headline: Europe unites on time, France poised to step back.

text.p: The 15 members of the European Union united for the first time over time on Sunday to put their clocks back one hour together -- but France is set to shatter the new-found harmony next year.
European countries had in the past changed to winter time on a confusing mixture of dates that played havoc with international airline timetables and border crossings.
Brussels spent years trying to synchronise the watch changes of all EU members. Their success could be shortlived.
For France now looks set to step out of line with its continental neighbours after a parliamentary report recommended abandoning the twice-yearly change of clocks.
The report recommended that France fix its clocks at one hour ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), currently the winter time in most EU nations.
The EU states currently put clocks forward an hour in summer under a policy aimed at saving energy and creating long summer evenings.
French reports say, however, that energy savings are minimal in summer time and that farmers, truck drivers and children leaving for school would benefit from lighter mornings.
Britons, who on Sunday put their clocks back one hour to be in line with Greenwich Mean Time for the winter, contemplated tinkering with time earlier this year. But the plan was abandoned.
In January, Prime Minister John Major bowed to pressure from Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth and scuppered a bill designed to bring clocks forward by one hour throughout the year.
Member of parliament John Butterfill argued that the change, that would have made evenings lighter and early mornings darker, could have slashed road casualties by up to 2,000 a year.
Butterfill also argued that advancing clocks an hour -- moving Britain to Central European Time with "double summer time" - would save 250 million pounds ($400 million) in heating and lighting bills.
But postmen and farmers argued they would face darker mornings when they started work outdoors and Forsyth complained that the winter sun in Scotland would not rise until nearly 10 in the morning.
